labels.dispersionHint: Random velocity change applied to each fragment. In-track stretches the cloud along the orbit; cross-track fans it across the orbital plane; radial raises and lowers it. Typical mean speeds: explosions about 10 to 100 m/s, collisions about 100 to 300 m/s.
labels.axis1_rtn_tooltip: Along the position vector, away from Earth. Raises and lowers the fragments.
labels.axis2_rtn_tooltip: In the orbital plane, perpendicular to radial, toward the direction of motion. Stretches the cloud along the orbit.
labels.axis3_rtn_tooltip: Along the orbit normal (r × v). Fans the cloud across the orbital plane.
labels.axis1_ntw_tooltip: In the orbital plane, perpendicular to the velocity and pointing outward. Matches radial on a circular orbit.
labels.axis2_ntw_tooltip: Along the velocity vector. Changes the orbital energy (period) most directly.
labels.axis3_ntw_tooltip: Along the orbit normal (r × v). The same axis as RTN cross-track.
labels.axis1_eci_tooltip: Inertial TEME X axis, toward the vernal equinox.
labels.axis2_eci_tooltip: Inertial TEME Y axis, 90° east of X in the equatorial plane.
labels.axis3_eci_tooltip: Inertial TEME Z axis, toward the celestial north pole.
labels.unitTooltip_gaussian: The value is the 1σ standard deviation of a zero-mean Gaussian on this axis.
labels.unitTooltip_maxwellian: Isotropic: every axis uses the σ derived from the mean ejection speed.
labels.unitTooltip_uniform: The value is the half-width: each fragment is drawn evenly between -max and +max on this axis.
labels.meanSpeedTooltip: Target mean of the total speed |Δv|. Each axis is drawn from a Gaussian with σ = μ / 1.596, so the total speed follows a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.
labels.maxTotalSpeedTooltip: Optional. Fragments whose total random Δv exceeds this value are redrawn, which trims the extreme tail without distorting the rest of the distribution. Leave blank for no cap.

help.overview: The Breakup menu simulates a satellite breaking apart at its current position. It spawns debris pieces from the selected satellite's exact location, each leaving with a small random velocity change (delta-V), so you can watch the debris cloud form and spread over time. Because it works from the satellite's state vector, it supports any orbital regime.
help.imgAlt: The Breakup menu with delta-V dispersion and piece-count controls
help.imgCaption: Breakup parameters. Larger delta-V values spread the simulated debris cloud wider.
help.parameters:
• Radial: velocity spread toward and away from Earth (m/s), which raises and lowers the fragments.
  • In-Track: velocity spread along the direction of motion (m/s), which stretches the cloud along the orbit.
  • Cross-Track: velocity spread out of the orbital plane (m/s), which fans the cloud across the plane.
  • Pieces: how many debris fragments to create (5 to 1000).
  • Initial Satellite Number: the first analyst catalog number to assign to the pieces (defaults to 90000).
The values are treated as a one-sigma spread per fragment. The defaults (about 40 m/s per axis) model an explosion-class event; real explosion fragments spread by roughly 10 to 100 m/s, while catastrophic collisions reach roughly 100 to 300 m/s (small fragments can exceed 1 km/s). Keep the three axes equal for a physically realistic, spherically symmetric event; the cloud naturally stretches along the orbit over time.
help.howToUse:
1. Select any satellite. The icon stays disabled until a satellite is selected.
  2. Open the Breakup menu and adjust the delta-V dispersion and piece count.
  3. Click Create Breakup. The pieces are generated at the satellite's current position and the search bar fills with the new debris so you can see the whole cloud.
  4. Speed up time to watch the cloud disperse along the orbit.
help.tip1: Works in any orbital regime, including LEO, MEO, GEO, and highly elliptical (HEO) orbits, because every fragment is propagated from the parent's state vector at the breakup point.
help.tip2: The breakup is simulated and in-memory only. Use Clear Breakup to remove the debris, or reload the page. The parent satellite itself is never modified.
help.tip3: All pieces are created as debris-type objects, so debris-based color schemes and filters apply to them immediately.
help.dispersionModels:
• Coordinate Frame: RTN / RIC (default) uses radial, in-track (transverse) and cross-track axes. NTW aligns the second axis with the velocity vector, which differs from RTN on eccentric orbits. ECI applies the values directly to the inertial X, Y and Z axes (TEME, the frame SGP4 uses).
  • Gaussian (default): each axis is drawn independently from a zero-mean normal distribution with the entered 1σ. With the same σ on all three axes, the total speed follows a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution with mean 2σ√(2/π) ≈ 1.596σ, so 54.2 m/s per axis gives a mean speed of 86.5 m/s.
  • Isotropic Maxwellian: enter the target mean ejection speed directly and the per-axis σ is derived for you.
  • Uniform: each axis is drawn evenly between -max and +max.
  • Max Total Speed (optional): fragments faster than the cap are redrawn, which removes outliers and keeps the shape of the distribution below the cap.
The readout under the inputs shows the expected mean, RMS and 99th-percentile speed before you create the breakup. Fragments whose new orbit has a perigee below 100 km are reported as reentered and are not created.
